articles.title_orig: Before news of his spy-linked affair, Jensen Huang said Nvidia “could be of great service” to China
articles.title_zh: Before news of his spy-linked affair, Jensen Huang said Nvidia “could be of great service” to China
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing an internal investigation after admitting to an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence agencies believe is a Chinese spy.
While the company has not yet named specific investigators, that probe is being helmed by the board with help from outside counsel, according to Nvidia. Lawyer Stephen Neal is the board's lead independent director and head of corporate governance, likely making him a key figure in the investigation.
In a statement , Nvidia's board said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised," though it will examine all evidence. China has dismissed the espionage claims. Huang, one of the most powerful businessmen in the artificial intelligence boom, said he would "cooperate fully" with the process.
Yet the probe has sparked uncertainty around Huang's future at the chipmaker and raised concerns of broader ripple effects to companies in the tech sector that are exposed to the AI build-out.
In a Monday note, Citi analysts wrote that one of the key issues for investors moving forward will be "potential governance implications" and "increased regulatory scrutiny" as the company navigates the investigation.
Nvidia's board has 10 independent members, including a former president of Taco Bell , a former Eli Lilly executive and a former vice chairman from Goldman Sachs . Neal, who joined Nvidia's board of directors in 2019, is a chairman emeritus and senior counsel of the law firm Cooley LLP, where he also served as CEO from 2001 to 2008.
Neal did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
It won't be his first corporate governance probe. According to Cooley , Neal has litigated cases across securities, bankruptcies, antitrust, takeovers and more. And he's conducted several investigations for multiple boards of directors, including at General Motors , where he advised the company in disputes with Ross Perot.
He also guided Walter Hewlett and the Hewlett Trust to stop a merger between Hewlett-Packard Co. and Compaq Computer Corp. and helped PacifiCare Health Systems with transactional matters.
According to the firm, Neal has conducted several investigations for committees of directors and independent directors, though most of those client names are confidential. He's also handled investigations with the Securities and Exchange Commission for both corporations and individuals.
When he joined Nvidia, Neal was also the chairman of the board of directors at Levi Strauss & Co . He stepped down in 2021 after reaching the mandatory board retirement age of 72, the company said at the time. The retailer did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC on Monday.
Cooley has a long history with Nvidia, too. The law firm said it incorporated the company in 1993 and has served as its principal outside corporate and litigation counsel for roughly three decades. Cooley handled Nvidia's initial public offering in 1999.
Investors will be closely watching the investigation, and its emphasis on independence, as the process unfolds, according to Brayden King, a professor of management and organizations at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management.
"You definitely want somebody leading it who people can look at and say, 'OK, we believe this is a report that we can fully believe and trust that the outcome is the right outcome,'" King told CNBC. "That's what investors are looking for. They just don't like the instability that comes with all of this."
King said the Nvidia investigation lies at a unique intersection of Wall Street and Washington, D.C., where the company is likely navigating its next steps to try to appease both groups.
Because Nvidia's reputation is highly correlated with Huang's reputation, King said, conducting a transparent investigation will be key to regaining and retaining shareholders' trust. Not having an immediate CEO succession plan in place is only impeding that confidence, he added.
"I think the board realizes that they're doing an independent investigation in part because they really need to understand to what extent there are real problems here, and they also know that if they don't do an independent investigation, then there will be lingering concerns about whether their key stakeholders can trust the company," King said.
If the investigation shows that national security was indeed put at risk, King said, the company will need to take "very strong measures" to restore its reputation.
"That will basically come down to having to put structures in place in corporate governance to assure that this can't happen again," King said. "The independent review is going to have to be truly independent, and it's going to have to be candid enough that people believe that we can restore some normalcy around how the company operates."
It's also likely influencing how other tech companies, particularly those in the AI space, are thinking about their own corporate governance structures and how they might navigate increased scrutiny on their leaders, he added.
Marcel Kahan, a professor of law at New York University, said he's not surprised that Nvidia has been potentially exposed to industrial espionage.
Because the company operates in such a high-visibility and crucial sector, Kahan said companies like Nvidia have to be careful in their operations and whom they trust with their information. The investigation could mean the company may consider adding additional governance committees to ensure this doesn't happen again.
The revelations about its CEO will also likely mean more specialized training from Nvidia and its law firms to ensure trade secrets are kept close.
He also said the company is likely prioritizing an in-depth investigation over transparency to investors, focusing on recruiting "the best of the best" to assist with the probe.
"Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies on Wall Street," Kahan told CNBC. "I think, given all the attention that's being paid to it, this is one of the instances where I would not be that worried about anything being done in an underhanded way."
Still, although Nvidia is a major company with massive influence on the market, the controversy may not end up making too large of a dent in corporate governance structures, according to Kathryn Harrigan, a professor of business leadership at Columbia Business School.
Harrigan said because Wall Street and Silicon Valley have seen similar controversies play out before, this scandal may simply be following the script of its predecessors.
"Is it going to change the basic structure of the AI build-out? Probably not," she told CNBC. "You sometimes wait years to get on their schedule if you have an order for chips. It's not like you can magically switch from one vendor to another."

On Kalshi , speculators say there's just a 17% chance Huang is gone by 2027. Those odds rise to 30% by 2028, and 35% by 2029. However, they think there is a 75% probability that Huang will depart by 2031.
Contracts on Huang's departure on Kalshi are resolved using information from Bloomberg.

Shares of Nvidia were down more than 5% after the news on Monday.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls 5% as board investigates CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls 5% as board investigates CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang’s close relationship with president means Nvidia CEO’s affair with woman alleged to be working for Beijing is a big deal
A hand on the back, a kiss on the cheek; the footage of Alice Huang’s interaction with Jensen Huang in a Taipei venue last year does not seem particularly remarkable at first glance.
But the Nvidia chief executive’s revelation on Sunday that he had an affair with Ms Huang has given it new significance.
According to reports, his lover, who is not a relation, was not just an executive at an Nvidia customer. She was also an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia has now launched an independent investigation into reports that the boss of a cornerstone company in the global AI boom has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
“While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” said the board.
Huang, 63, a poster boy of the AI boom in his trademark leather jacket, admitted there was “no excuse” for what he had done.
Aside from Huang’s dented personal reputation, what is the scale of the damage done to Nvidia and US national security?
The story started to emerge last year when the New York Times and Bloomberg raised questions about a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia’s powerful chips, which have become the proverbial shovels in the AI gold rush. There were concerns that Megaspeed was flouting US restrictions on AI chip exports to China by diverting some Nvidia inventory to America’s arch AI rival. Nvidia and Megaspeed denied this.
Then last month came a further startling NYT report that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, and that American officials believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Donald Trump had been told, but decided not to act on the information. It is now evident that the relationship was more than just close.
At the heart of the question of what China might have achieved through Alice Huang is the extremely close relationship between the CEO of the world’s second-most-valuable company and the president of the United States.
The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia appeared to have successfully leaned on the US commerce department to halt an investigation into potential chip smuggling on the part of Megaspeed. That pressure came through a Trump appointee, who allowed Nvidia to reach out about the case.
Responding to reports last year that it might have diverted Nvidia deliveries, Megaspeed said: “Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company, operating fully in compliance with all applicable laws, including US export control regulations.”
Trump has met frequently – at least seven times – with the head of Nvidia since the start of his second term. Huang has flown on Air Force One and taken calls from the president during public events.
Four of their meetings have touched on one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relationships: the controls that the US has put up around the export of the world’s most advanced AI chips, which are almost entirely sold by Nvidia.
Under the former president Joe Biden, the US put in place the Chips Act, a package of rules that introduced sweeping limitations on US tech companies and their overseas trading partners. These rules sought to control what semiconductor technologies US companies could sell to businesses based overseas – particularly those that might be put under pressure to transfer those technologies to China.
It also introduced strict licensing requirements that in turn limited what those partners could do with technology that they bought.
For Nvidia, this was bad for business. China was one of the largest markets for its GPU chips – accounting for roughly a quarter of its revenue in the years between 2020 and 2022. When the Chips Act passed, the company started to sell downgraded versions of its premier chips to China – for example , the A800 and H800. Some of these were then banned, forcing Nvidia to scramble even more.
Under Trump, things changed. The president first invited Huang to the White House just six days after he was inaugurated, to discuss AI policy and chip exports . The two then met again in July and August of 2025. This was followed by victories for Huang – Trump allowed Nvidia to export previously banned chips to China. Nvidia agreed, in turn, to give the US government 15% of the sales revenue.
Experts said the deal would help Beijing compete “on the AI frontier”, in other words develop AI systems to rival those being produced by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI.
Five months later, the tech boss appeared to win another startling concession, days after another meeting with Trump. The president agreed to allow the tech boss to export H200s – a far more powerful chip – to China, in exchange for 25% of the revenue.
“President Xi responded positively!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
It is not unusual for large technology companies to lobby for their preferred policies in Washington; nor is it unusual for Trump to give access – and favourable deals – to men he likes.
But one more thing is now apparent – during this crucial year for his company, Huang was also intimately involved with a reported Chinese spy. The two were first photographed together in mid-2024. Five months after Trump took office is when the two were filmed at the Taipei restaurant. This would have been at the height of Huang’s lobbying push, shortly before Trump agreed to let Nvidia sell the H200s.
What could Alice Huang have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair? Plenty. Glimpses into US policy as it was being made, and to Trump’s own chaotic thinking on AI. And perhaps a world of tips beyond the confines of the White House.
Huang was a key figure for government after government as they formulated their AI policy. He met world leaders from South Korea to Saudi Arabia that year; he joined the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, on stage in London.
He would have known the details of the most important tech policy for many governments on Earth – their AI ambitions – because his company was often the only one that could make these ambitions happen. That is certainly true for Britain.
For all the intellectual feats of the systems powered by Nvidia technology, it is Huang’s human intelligence that is most valuable to America’s competitors.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic releases first frontier models since Amodei's call for slowdown as IPO buzz builds
articles.title_zh: Anthropic releases first frontier models since Amodei's call for slowdown as IPO buzz builds
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic on Monday released two new artificial intelligence models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, as the company readies for a potentially historic IPO that could take place as soon as next week.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are Anthropic's most advanced offerings, and the company said they generate outputs 30% faster than their predecessors. The models also cost 20% less than the 5.1 generation, and will be available for $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, the company said.
The launch marks the first time that Anthropic has released so-called "frontier" models since its CEO, Dario Amodei , called to slow down the pace of AI development in September . Anthropic said the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release.
"We called for pacing, not pausing," Dianne Penn, Anthropic's head of product management for research, told CNBC in an interview.
Anthropic has to balance its safety efforts with intense commercial and competitive pressures, a tension that the company highlighted in the extensive risk factors section of its prospectus late last month. And as executives prepare to kick off Anthropic's IPO roadshow , they'll have to convince investors that their approach is the right one.
The company is aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion in its offering, as CNBC previously reported , down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.
Anthropic first introduced Mythos in April, and it limited the rollout to a select group of organizations because of the model's advanced cybersecurity capabilities. The company introduced Fable , a publicly available version of Mythos with additional safeguards, two months later.
The models — particularly Mythos — captivated Wall Street and government officials alike, and they helped to fuel Anthropic's meteoric rise this year. The company said in its amended prospectus that it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year.
Penn said Fable 5.2 is primarily intended for "power users or power use cases" since it excels at complex, open-ended technical work. Other models like Claude Opus 5.5 , which Anthropic released in September, are better suited for daily tasks, so Penn said users should turn to Fable 5.2 when they need to tackle hard problems in engineering, mathematics and robotics.
"These are just net new things that are completely novel, and so they're frontier use cases," Penn said. "We expect that over time to maybe trickle to the Opus class, but really right now we do see a difference in terms of performance that we think those frontier use cases benefit from."
Anthropic said Fable 5.2 is generally available on Monday, and Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations through the company's Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

articles.title_orig: October inflation data is expected to be cooler, helped by steadying energy prices
articles.title_zh: October inflation data is expected to be cooler, helped by steadying energy prices
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
October inflation data coming on Tuesday is expected to show that inflation cooled somewhat from September's elevated levels but remains sticky.
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the Consumer Price Index to rise 0.3% in October compared to a month earlier, a far slower pace than September's 0.6% gain. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, is seen rising 0.2%, down from 0.3% a month earlier.
October's report is unlikely to include annual inflation figures because the Bureau of Labor Statistics was unable to publish full October 2025 data due to the government shutdown last year. But some economists estimate that inflation accelerated slightly on a year-over-year basis.
Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation
Rising energy prices weighed heavily on September's report , but October's price increases look less dramatic.
"We expect more subdued CPI in October after two straight disappointing 0.3% gains in the core rate," Dave Sloan, senior economist for North America at Continuum Economics, wrote in a note. "Gasoline prices have seen only a marginal rise on the month, and we expect overall CPI to also rise by 0.2%."
Inflation on many goods likely eased last month as tariff pressures faded, though goods inflation has been running hot in recent months due to intense artificial intelligence demand and rising vehicle prices, Bank of America economist Stephen Juneau wrote in a note. Services inflation is likely sticky due to factors like rising airfare prices, he added.
"Although we expect monthly core CPI to moderate, we see the risks as skewed to the upside," the note said. "The two biggest sources of uncertainty are used cars and health insurance."
Tuesday's inflation data is the Federal Reserve's final look at the CPI before it meets Dec. 8-9, although it will get another look at inflation data via its preferred measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, later this month.
With the labor market holding up , and even showing signs of accelerating, traders currently see an 83% chance that the central bank raises benchmark interest rates by 25 basis points. Another sticky inflation report is likely to cement those odds.

articles.title_orig: Claude can design electronic prototypes from start to finish
articles.title_zh: Claude can design electronic prototypes from start to finish
articles.content_orig:
A little over a year ago, we began testing how well Claude could design basic electronic circuits. We collaborated with Diode Computers , 1 a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards, to train Claude on simple tasks—for example, on reading a chip’s datasheet and working out which parts a chip needs in order to run. The models we experimented with back then couldn’t reliably lay out a circuit board; they also struggled to design components that fit together. Now, Claude can both design and prototype electronic hardware from start to finish.
Engineering an electronic device requires working through many complex steps and practical constraints. You have to not only design and simulate a circuit board, but also reason about the board’s physical layout and how it will behave, model the mechanical components, and write firmware—all while keeping track of which parts are readily available and what a factory is set up to build.
To see how newer Claude models have improved in this area, we collaborated with Diode again, this time asking Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. With minimal prompting, Claude was able to use geometric reasoning to lay out each circuit board, anticipate manufacturing constraints, and make sure its designs would work within them. It revised its own work, modeled its designs in computer-aided design (CAD) software, and, finally, directed human engineers to build prototypes that worked without any fixes to their circuitry.
For each design, we began by giving Claude a simple prompt that outlined what kind of device to build and its main hardware requirements. The prompt for the speakerphone, for example, asked for “a puck that plugs into a computer over USB-C and includes microphones and a speaker, supporting Bluetooth with a PCB antenna.” Claude proceeded to write the device’s specifications, draw clean visual schematics, choose where to place the components on a printed circuit board (PCB), route the copper connections between them, design a 3D-printable enclosure, code the firmware, and prepare a parts list. Diode assembled the circuit boards and ran the firmware, under Claude’s direction. The final result was a prototype of a speakerphone that still works after weeks of use.
Claude went through a similar process to build the voice-assistant hub and the virtual pet, and both are also still in good working order. Because the devices are early prototypes, we don’t yet know how they’ll hold up with continued use or whether they would pass commercial certifications.
The most substantial difference between Fable 5.2 and the models we used in our earlier tests was in how well Fable 5.2 reasoned through complex geometric problems, such as where to place components on a circuit board and how to route the copper connections between them.
Earlier models had struggled to decide how to arrange basic components—placing supporting parts too far from the chips they served, for example, or orienting connectors incorrectly. Fable 5.2, by contrast, produced more compact, practical layouts. It routed the most important connections first: those that carry high-speed signals or high currents, or that are sensitive to noise. For example, for the voice-assistant hub, Claude started by routing the USB and Ethernet connections, which transmit signals along pairs of tracks—thin strips of copper on the board. It routed one pair of tracks at a time, keeping the two tracks in each pair the same length and correctly spaced. It also added tuning patterns—small zigzags that lengthen a track so that signals arrive at the same time—and arranged the parts of the power supply to make it more efficient.
To demonstrate how much better Fable 5.2 is than earlier models at laying out circuit boards, we asked Diode to run PCB Gym—an internal benchmark that scores models based on how well they can place components and reroute connections on board designs whose layouts have been removed. Fable 5.2 scored 69% on the benchmark, compared with 25% for Fable 5 (Figure 2). It also performed better on BenchCAD 2.1 , a public benchmark that tests whether models can rebuild 3D parts, assemblies, and circuit boards from engineering drawings and rendered images. Fable 5.2 scored 83.5%, nearly double the score of its predecessor, Claude Fable 5.1.
Earlier models rarely revised their own work when designing PCB layouts, even when it became clear that their placement choices would never let them finish routing the connections. Over the past year, Diode designed many boards with these models that were 95% complete but still unusable.
When Claude noticed one of its designs wasn’t working, it would change course without being prompted to do so. For instance, when designing the speakerphone’s circuit board, which has four layers of copper, it reassigned signals to different pins on two of the chips. This allowed the tracks under the speakerphone’s touch-sensitive controls to stay on a single layer without crossing one another. Later, when the back of the board became too crowded, Claude swapped the signals on interchangeable pins and laid out a whole corner of the board again, rather than patching the problem with extra jumps between layers.
And when placing tracks in its design file for the voice-assistant hub, Claude noticed that the copper connections were “getting too tangled to trace visually” and reasoned, “I should just rip these traces [tracks] and start fresh.” It proceeded to delete and reroute copper connections dozens of times until it found an arrangement that worked.
When a design decision for one of the devices depended on the details of a particular part, Claude often checked that part’s datasheet—a technical document published by the manufacturer. When asked whether the handheld pet would work without a battery, Claude read the charger’s datasheet and answered that it would run on USB power but predicted that the charging light would flicker, because the charger keeps recharging a small capacitor in the battery’s place. 2
To route the connections on the voice-assistant hub, Claude started with the design software Diode provided, which let it run the router (a tool for drawing tracks) built into KiCad, a widely used circuit board design program. KiCad’s router drew one track at a time between two points Claude chose. But the hub had long tracks running from a 100-pin connector, and Claude judged that routing these one by one would take too much step-by-step guidance.
Instead, Claude wrote its own router: an algorithm that divides the board into a grid and searches it to find a clear path for each track. Within about half an hour, Claude had a router that could lay each long track in roughly a second. When Claude spotted an audio clock track running too close to the Ethernet tracks, it adjusted the router to leave more room around sensitive tracks.
Decisions made in one part of a design have downstream effects, which Claude kept track of. While designing each device’s enclosure, it wrote code to check that a 3D model of the circuit board would fit inside the enclosure without any components colliding. For example, it found that the speakerphone’s board couldn’t be lowered straight into the enclosure, because the mute switch would hit the back wall. Claude worked out that the board would fit if it was tilted by about 25 degrees during installation. It tested this in its 3D model and added the step to the assembly instructions.
When designing the enclosure for the voice-assistant hub, Claude calculated that a 25 mm-long microphone port—the opening that lets sound reach the microphone—would resonate near 3.4 kHz. That is “right in the voice band,” it reasoned, “which is not ideal though still usable for voice assistant purposes. A better approach is a wedge-shaped enclosure that’s tall at the rear and steps down low at the front.” The wedge shape shortened the ports to about 10 mm, which

A fresh round of peace talks between the US, Ukraine and Russia are set to begin Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, as the Trump administration renews its drive to end the nearly five-year conflict even after it announced significant concessions to Moscow.
Russia has made clear it wants the negotiations – the first of their kind since February – to be strictly trilateral, though national security advisers from several European nations, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union, are also expected in the UAE capital for separate meetings.
“We are working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine,” US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner said Monday.
US officials on Monday underlined that posture, saying that the upcoming talks are a new starting point in defining an end to the war, including discussions on security guarantees and a “post-war security architecture.”
“We need to come up with a way that, when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war, and we believe that’s what Ukraine wants. We believe that’s what Europe wants and we believe that’s what Russia wants,” one official said.
However, many – particularly in Europe – have cast doubt on Moscow’s intentions. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said Monday she saw little sign that Russia was willing to negotiate in good faith.
Meanwhile, the US official also said that it would be up to Trump to decide whether to offer a US security guarantee as part of peace talks.
The US will be represented by Kushner and Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff, while Ukraine’s foreign intelligence chief and top negotiator Rustem Umerov will lead the Ukrainian delegation, according to the official with knowledge of the talks.
Russia is sending deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin as delegates, according to Russian state news agency TASS, as well as Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and member of general staff Yuri Zhigarlovsky.
Representatives from the E4 group – the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy – as well as officials from NATO and the European Commission will also be in Abu Dhabi, Umerov said Monday. “We will hold separate coordination meetings with our European partners,” Umerov added.
Asked about the presence of European officials in Abu Dhabi, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Europe has its own channels of communication with Kyiv and Washington, while reaffirming that the talks are “a trilateral negotiation – involving Russia and Ukraine – with the United States acting as a mediator.”
Notably, these talks come amid a renewed push by European nations for a more active role in negotiations over Ukraine’s future, and the security of the bloc at large, after Trump touted a new security deal for Ukraine that “might involve all of Europe.”
“The Europeans will be well represented,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told French media Sunday. “In recent weeks, the Europeans have made their voices heard. They have expressed to the American mediator that no discussion affecting the future of the continent can ignore our expectations and demands,” he added.
Europe has long been wary of any US-brokered peace deal negotiated without its involvement, with Umerov saying Monday that Ukraine was “doing everything we can to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process.”
While the talks will remain trilateral, Kushner said that he and Witkoff would also meet with European partners to continue the “close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine’s postwar future over the past several weeks.”
“Ultimately, achieving a comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them,” Kushner posted on X.
This will be the fourth round of trilateral talks. All have ended without significant breakthrough.
Earlier this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the most recent trilateral talks in Geneva, Switzerland, in February fell short of Ukraine’s goals, saying “sensitive political matters, issues of possible compromises and the necessary meeting of leaders have not yet been sufficiently worked through.”
The US later postponed a round of trilateral talks that were expected to take place in March due to the war in Iran.
Putin is still making maximalist demands previously rejected by Kyiv, including Russian control over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, a reduction in the size of Ukraine’s military and the abandonment of Kyiv’s ambitions to join NATO.
John Herbst, senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and a former US ambassador to Ukraine, said any expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks should be “very modest.”
“They are only taking place because Putin wants to give Trump a reason to continue to distance himself from Ukraine,” Herbst wrote last week .
With Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year and gains on the battlefield remaining difficult to come by, Moscow has escalated its aerial attacks – with deadly results for Ukrainians.
At least 55 people were killed last Monday when Russia dropped several bombs on a school building used as a shelter and aid center in Zaporizhzhia , marking one of the deadliest single incidents of the war to date. Civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest point since the start of the war, with more than 2,700 killed in Russian strikes so far this year, according to ACLED, a global conflict monitor.
And continuing a pattern seen in previous years, Russian drones and missiles are already hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, but harder and earlier than in other winters, analysts say. Russian attacks on the power grid left more than 600,000 people in the Dnipropetrovsk region without electricity overnight into Sunday, Zelensky said, as temperatures plummet and winter draws in.
Over the past few months, Russia has deployed faster, jet-powered Shahed drones, which are harder to shoot down. At the same time, more missiles are slipping through Ukraine’s air defenses as Kyiv grapples with a chronic shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors that are one of the few defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.
Where the Biden administration positioned the US as Ukraine’s biggest single donor and most powerful ally, the Trump administration’s relationship with Kyiv has been decidedly more complicated. It halted financial aid to Ukraine at the beginning of 2025, while the intelligence and technology support it still provides has come under strain in recent weeks too.
Last month, Zelensky accused his Western allies of not providing intelligence warnings before multiple ballistic missile attacks, a claim that the Trump administration denied.
In October too, Ukraine’s ability to use Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is critical to its military operations, was hampered when speed limits were imposed on the satellite terminals. Trump denied approving that decision, while Musk said the Trump administration was behind the ban in a social media post.
Undergirding all this recent tension has been Trump’s sensitivity to rising gas prices, which skyrocketed due to the Iran war and contributed to the Republicans’ landslide defeat in last week’s midterms.
He has shown a willingness to strike business deals with Moscow, including one to supply markets with Russia’s diesel, in a sharp break from the sanctions aimed at punishing and isolating the Russian economy, and pressured Zelensky to accept a short-lived “energy ceasefire.”

The clue that matters most is sitting in his hand. Zoom in on the shot and Kodak Black is holding a cup branded with the Jack of Hearts logo, tying him directly to one of GTA VI’s in-game clubs. Jack of Hearts has been a recurring presence throughout Rockstar’s promotional rollout, and Travis Scott even worked the venue’s name into “RHYNO,” a track he recorded specifically for the game’s soundtrack.
That connection is fueling the bigger question. Fans have long suspected the club would serve as a hub for recognizable artists, and a confirmed Kodak Black sighting makes the theory much harder to dismiss. Scott is the obvious next candidate, though any of the rappers lined up for the official soundtrack could plausibly surface inside the venue. Rockstar has not confirmed any additional appearances.
There is also a strong hometown logic to the casting. Kodak Black hails from Pompano Beach, Florida, and GTA VI’s state of Leonida is the series’ take on Florida, making him a natural fit for the setting.
The franchise has a track record that backs up the speculation. GTA Online’s 2018 After Hours update turned real DJs including Solomun, Tale Of Us, Dixon and The Black Madonna into resident performers at player-owned nightclubs, a template that maps neatly onto a venue like Jack of Heart. Rockstar pushed the idea further in 2021 with The Contract , which cast Dr. Dre as himself at the center of a full storyline. articles.title_zh: France, U.S. Suspect Iran Was Behind Cyberattack on European Fridges
articles.content_orig:
France is blaming Iran for last month’s supermarket refrigerator cyberattack . which spoiled produce at around 700 retailers, and is vowing to slap sanctions on Tehran in response.
“This was an attack of unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggressiveness,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told reporters Monday. He described it as the first large-scale cyberattack carried out for sabotage purposes on French national territory.
“It represents a major assault on the nation’s interests and on the security of the French people,” Barrot said. France has summoned Iran’s ambassador and intends to impose retaliatory sanctions “at a European level,” he added.
There was no immediate comment from Tehran on the French allegations.
The cyberattack in October occurred when hackers remotely connected to supermarket refrigerators and freezers, then raised their temperature by switching on defrost cycles, according to CNN affiliate BFMTV. That led to the loss of large quantities of fresh and frozen produce and even caused some of the refrigeration equipment to catch fire.
The Paris prosecutor’s office took up the case and on Monday accused Iran of being behind the attack, citing “the use of Farsi and IP addresses pointing to devices located in Iran.”
The prosecutor’s office said it has opened an investigation into the head of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, as well as his two deputies and any other individuals responsible.
A similar cyberattack targeted supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium and Ireland earlier this month, though it remains unclear if the incidents are linked to the one in France. No one has claimed responsibility for this month’s cyberattacks in other European countries.
Shortly after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February, the US intelligence community issued a flurry of private warnings to American companies and government agencies urging vigilance amid the threat of possible cyberattacks from Iran, according to national security sources and memos reviewed by CNN.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife” and took "full responsibility" for his actions.
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The company said that while its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information.
It said that the board has confidence in Huang and his ⁠leadership team, adding that the CEO fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
Late last month, the New York Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.
Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.
When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against the Asian country.
Trump said on Sunday he had not spoken to Huang about ​the allegations, but ⁠called him a fine person.
"I hope everything's fine. He's done such an ‌incredible job," he added.
When asked if he believed he should have acted on intelligence when he was briefed about it, Trump said: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it."
Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
However, the investigation adds to pressure on Nvidia at a time investors are already pulling back amid uncertainty over the sustainability of the booming AI market.
Nvidia shares fell in out-of-hours trading on Monday and extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference set to begin this week.
But Seoul expects contracted deliveries of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) to proceed without disruption despite a controversy surrounding Huang. Vice Minister of Science and ICT Ryu Jemyung told a parliamentary budget committee that 10,000 GPUs funded under a 2025 supplementary budget had already arrived and were in use.
Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday that “today’s news will not slow Nvidia”. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”
Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to say whether Huang was excluded from U.S. briefings in light of the recent reporting. He told reporters Sunday before departing for France, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.”
Trump is a major backer of AI, trying to rebrand the technology as SI for “Super Intelligence” and loosen regulations.
While Huang may be an ally to the president, it will be hard to overlook a potential security breach from not only a U.S. adversary, but also its top competitor in the AI race.
“We’re leading China in AI,” the president said in September amid concerns that AI could pose an existential threat to humans . “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an "incredible human," but if "indeed this is more ⁠than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem."
"I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he added.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk commented "I agree" on a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad for America" but that "Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership".
The Independent has reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Opens Investigation Into Jensen Huang’s Relationship With Suspected Chinese Spy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Opens Investigation Into Jensen Huang’s Relationship With Suspected Chinese Spy
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 6% on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying "allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report , external .
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.
Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (Â£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened on a positive note on Monday after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so central to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

articles.title_zh: China’s rare-earth rubber trades at 22,500 yuan a tonne, about 35% above standard rubber
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
China is testing whether a premium rubber can win a place in electric-vehicle tires. Rare-earth cis-butadiene rubber, made with a rare-earth catalyst, now has a Xinjiang plant rated at 100,000 metric tons a year, about 110,000 U.S. tons. It also trades at a higher price than conventional synthetic rubber.
China Rubber Industry Association data published Nov. 2 quoted rare-earth grade ND9106 at 22,500 yuan (about US$3,400) per metric ton during Oct. 26 to Nov. 1. Conventional BR9000 in Shandong province was quoted at 16,660 yuan per metric ton, so the rare-earth grade carried a premium of about 35%.
For tire makers, the rubber offers better wear resistance, greater strength and lower rolling resistance, and wider domestic production could make it more widely available.
A production unit at Dushanzi Petrochemical Company in Karamay, Xinjiang, completed a successful trial run on June 27, producing premium-grade rare-earth cis-butadiene rubber. The Chinese Academy of Sciences' Changchun Institute of Applied Chemistry announced the result on July 16.
The institute called the achievement a "major breakthrough" and said the core technologies are "fully under domestic control." It said the project would help meet "urgent demand for high-end grades ," support the petrochemical new-materials industry and help "safeguard supply-chain security."
The process makes two national-standard grades, BR1240 and BR1260, which differ in Mooney viscosity, a standard measure of rubber viscosity and processability. The rubber is made by polymerizing butadiene with a rare-earth catalyst, which helps control the polymer's molecular structure and, in turn, its mechanical properties.
Electric cars tend to be heavier than comparable gasoline vehicles and deliver high torque during acceleration, which places greater demands on tire durability. Low rolling resistance reduces the energy lost as tires deform and roll, while wear and fatigue resistance can extend tire life under repeated stress.
Heavy-duty vehicles also benefit from rubber that can withstand high loads, repeated deformation and heat build-up. Greater resistance to tearing and fatigue can improve durability under demanding conditions.
The institute says the rare-earth version beats conventional nickel-based butadiene rubber on wear resistance, strength, fatigue and tear resistance, low-temperature performance, heat build-up and rolling resistance .
The same properties could matter for military tires and other high-performance rubber parts, though the institute has disclosed nothing about supplying weapons or military vehicles.
The industrial result builds on more than six decades of work at the institute. In 1964, scientists Ouyang Jun and Shen Zhiquan published a paper on rare-earth compounds as catalysts for stereospecific polymerization. The institute describes it as the first international publication on using rare-earth catalysts to produce butadiene rubber.
Work on stereospecific polymerization catalyzed by rare-earth complexes won second prize in China's National Natural Science Award in 1982. Researchers including Bi Jifu, Jiang Liansheng and Zhang Xuequan later ran thousands of scale-up experiments and dozens of pilot trials to develop an industrial process.
A second-generation process led by Bi adds automation and domestically developed technology and equipment. His team tackled precise control of catalyst structure, catalyst preparation, tolerance of different feedstocks, and the integration of long-chain branching and functionalization.
The institute says its work progressed from meeting urgent needs of the national economy to supporting national defense modernization. Earlier defense-related work included liquid polysulfide rubber used as a binder for composite solid propellants, which supported China's "two bombs, one satellite" program.

Apple’s generative AI service, Apple Intelligence, has been registered for use on tablets and laptops in China, Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator announced on Monday. The move expands the service beyond smartphones and follows the company’s earlier regulatory approval for iPhones in July 2026.
China requires companies to register large language models and generative AI services with authorities before offering them to the public. The latest filing adds iPads and Mac laptops as approved uses for the service, clearing a key step toward broader availability across Apple’s device lineup in the mainland market.
Apple has developed a China-specific large language model with support from Alibaba, marking a shift from its approach in other markets. Alibaba’s Qwen model will provide text and image understanding and content generation capabilities through features such as Siri, writing tools, and visual intelligence. Alibaba has stated that these capabilities will be available to Chinese users across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS.
The company has indicated that the features will arrive with the iOS 27.3 update in December 2026, following the release of a test version for developers on November 4. Earlier reporting has also noted involvement by Baidu in certain Apple Intelligence features for Chinese users.
The registration comes nearly two years after Apple Intelligence first launched in other markets, reflecting the time required to meet China’s regulatory standards for AI services. Expanding approval from iPhones to tablets and laptops is expected to support a more consistent AI experience across Apple’s ecosystem in China once the December rollout begins. ‎ MacDailyNews Take: Good news for Apple and for iPad and Mac sales in China, but as we wrote in November 2024 , “Apple Intelligence in China will be highly censored and rather limited; it will only spit back the approved narratives of the Chinese Communist Party.” The Chinese people are, unfortunately, acclimated to censorship and a lack of freedom, so iPad and Mac sales will increase with the advent of Apple Intelligence in China, regardless of the limitations placed upon it by the Chinese Communist Party.

articles.content_orig:
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”
Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.
At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna. Not only that, it’s cost-competitive with open source competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash.
Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness. In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”
With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio. The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.”
Ember is the fourth model released under Meta’s Muse brand, following the mid-weight Spark ( released in April ), Spark’s open source twin Glimmer ( released in August ), and the Wonder frontier model ( released in October ). The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.

articles.content_orig:
Just like the open-world entries that precede it, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 comes with a handful of HUD options, so you can play with as much or as little on-screen information as you please.
In our first few hours with the game, we played around with all three of these options, getting to grips with the pros and cons of all of them. Most of us settled on one after a little while, and now we're keen to see where you lovely lot have ended up.
As a reminder, there are three different HUD options in the settings menu's 'In-Game Interface Tab': Normal , Pro , and Master . The first of these is listed as your "Standard display," with your mini map, item selection, D-pad options, life/magic meters, and button prompts all appearing on the screen. It offers the most information you can get at a glance, but it can look a little cluttered for some.
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
The 'Pro' option tones things down a little, displaying "minimal information," according to its settings definition. This one does away with almost all the info we mentioned above, but button prompts (for 'Talk' or 'Grab' selections) and Navi's speech bubbles still make an appearance. This is a ripe choice for anyone who knows their Zelda mechanics, but still wants to know when something is there to be interacted with.
'Master' mode is the most stripped back of the bunch, offering a "display with no information". This means that everything other than the main gameplay is removed from the screen, and no prompts crop up as you approach NPCs or interactive items. And yes, that includes your targeting cursor. This option keeps things stripped back to the bare minimum and arguably provides the most immersive experience of the bunch, but there's every chance that you'll miss the odd detail (or Navi quip) along the way.
Each setting has its perks, to be sure, and we're not about to say that any one of them is the 'correct' way to play, but still, we're interested to know what mode you have been rocking with so far.
You can let us know your preferred HUD option in the following poll, then take to the comments to let us know why it's stuck.

Tom Boggioni is a writer, born, raised and living in San Diego — where he attended San Diego State University. Prior to writing for Raw Story, he wrote for FireDogLake, blogged as TBogg, and worked in banking, marketing and construction.
Democrats want answers from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh , demanding to know whether he is hiding secret conversations with Donald Trump .
The president says he and Warsh have talked. Warsh’s official records say they haven’t. And the Fed chair isn’t explaining the gap, the Washington Post reported.
On Friday, the Fed released Warsh’s September calendar, and once again, Trump’s name doesn’t appear. That makes "five months in a row," every month since Warsh took over in May, with no logged contact with the president. It comes despite a request this summer from Senate Democrats that he include any such conversations.
According to the Post, " The calendars are one of the few windows into how often a president reaches the official who leads the central bank’s decisions on interest rates , and previous Fed chairs have recorded interactions with presidents there. The Fed is designed to operate independently of the White House , setting rates based on its own best assessment of the economy rather than short-term political pressure."
On Sept. 16, the same day Warsh and his colleagues raised rates a quarter point against Trump’s wishes, the president told reporters he had weighed in on Warsh’s vote.
“I talked to Kevin, and I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board ’cause it’s not gonna matter,’” Trump said, noting that Warsh lacked the votes to change the outcome.
When a reporter asked if he had tried to sway Warsh, Trump said he hadn’t. “No, I didn’t convince him. No, I said, ‘Do what you want,’” he said, adding that he wanted Warsh “to be independent.”
Neither side has cleared it up, the report notes. The White House has refused to say when that conversation took place, and Warsh won’t confirm it ever happened.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) and three other Democratic senators wrote to Warsh in August, asking him to state in writing whether he had spoken with Trump and to correct his calendars if so. Van Hollen’s office told the Post on Friday that Warsh never replied.
“It’s clear neither Warsh nor Trump give a damn about transparency to the American people,” Van Hollen said. “Under a Democratic majority in Congress, we will continue pushing for that much-needed transparency.”

One day after the company filed for bankruptcy, the websites for The Children’s Place and its sub-brand, Gymboree, advertised “total inventory blowout” sales with steep discounts on in-store and online purchases.
The Children’s Place is also forecasting an untold number of store closures.
“At this time, all of our stores and e-commerce sites remain open and continue to serve customers,” a company spokesperson told Boston.com in an email. “With that said, The Children’s Place has determined that it will be necessary to close certain stores during this process.”
The spokesperson did not say whether these closures will include the 10 branches of The Children’s Place in Massachusetts.
“We are conducting an ongoing evaluation of our operational footprint and will communicate confirmed decisions as they are made,” they added, saying these “difficult decisions” are necessary to improve the company’s finances and give The Children’s Place “the best opportunity to move forward on stronger footing.”
According to bankruptcy filings in New Jersey, where The Children’s Place is headquarterd, the company “has experienced declining sales and profitability, competitive and promotional pressures, increased costs, and significant liquidity constraints.”
The Children’s Place’s then-executive chairman, Turki S. AlRajhi, addressed those financial woes in an April letter to shareholders as he reflected on Saudi investment firm and majority owner Mithaq Capital’s attempts to turn the company around.
“Our results fell short of what we expect of ourselves,” AlRajhi wrote. “While 2025 was a challenging year for most retailers—TCP is no exception—we are not pleased with the results, and we own it.”
AlRajhi stepped down as executive chairman last week, ahead of the bankruptcy filing.
In Sunday’s press release, Rudy Morando, co-chief restructuring officer for The Children’s Place, said bankruptcy is an “important step” in the company’s efforts to find the best path forward to financial stability.
“For nearly 60 years, The Children’s Place has supported growing families with apparel that customers have come to know and love,” Morando said. “We recognize the significance of this development for our employees, customers, vendors, and other partners, and we are committed to conducting an efficient and transparent sale process. In the meantime, we remain focused on serving the families who have trusted The Children’s Place for generations.”

NASA wants a base on the moon, and Wall Street is suddenly buying the ride there. Space stocks are ripping for a second session as SpaceX ( SPCX ) and seven other companies line up for lunar delivery work worth up to $10 billion.
NASA named the eight winners on Nov. 7 at Kennedy Space Center. Alongside SpaceX and Blue Origin are three smaller public companies, Intuitive Machines ( LUNR ), Firefly Aerospace ( FLY ) and Voyager Technologies ( VOYG ).
For those three, the prize is out of this world. They're worth about $8.5 billion combined, less than the contract's ceiling, though each still has to win missions one by one.
Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) is NASA's way of hiring private companies to fly cargo to the moon. The new 10-year version covers larger landers, and NASA raised the original contract's value to $4.2 billion from $2.6 billion. Intuitive Machines CEO Steve Altemus said the company is "excited to participate in this next evolution of CLPS."
"We are building the Moon Base mission by mission," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in the agency's announcement.
Rocket Lab ( RKLB ) didn't make NASA's list but is jumping ahead of reporting its third quarter results after Monday's close. The stock is on track for a two-day gain of nearly 30%, its third-best run in two years, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Space stocks are surging off last week's post-election low, up roughly 25% to 60% since the Nov. 5 close, with Firefly in the lead. SpaceX is on track for its best two-day run in a month, while the Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) has gained about 4%.
The bounce follows a brutal stretch. An average of nine space stocks more than doubled this year by May 28, two weeks before SpaceX's June 12 debut, then gave it all back. The group is now down for 2026.
SpaceX is a different story. Wall Street prices it less as a lunar trucker than as an AI cloud, competing with neoclouds — companies like CoreWeave ( CRWV ) that rent out AI computing power — and with hyperscalers, the cloud giants such as Amazon ( AMZN ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ).
On Monday, SpaceX added more than $100 billion in market value, more than the roughly $90 billion that 16 other US-listed space stocks are worth combined. NASA's 10-year moon pot is about a tenth of that one-day gain.
The next read on the rest of the group comes Monday night, when Rocket Lab reports and updates investors on Neutron, its bigger rocket targeted for a first flight this quarter.

Boeing said Monday that it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce as its production ramp-up is moving at a slower pace than the company expected.
The cuts will be through a combination of attrition and layoffs, Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, said in a memo to staff.
Pope reiterated that the company is still working to stabilize production rates of its bestselling 737 Max planes, which are made outside of Seattle.
CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors last month that the company won't significantly increase production of the Max aircraft until the second half of next year. He said the company's wing production has been slower than expected.
"Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position," Pope said in her note Monday. "Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business plan, resulting in a reduction of approximately 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December."
Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. Ortberg said the company has been trying to stabilize output at a rate of about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
